blocks.text: Rule given: "If P, then Q." Only two moves are safe.
Example: "If it is a holiday, the bank is closed. The bank is open." → It is not a holiday (row 2).
"The bank is closed, so it is a holiday" is the classic trap (row 3): the bank may close for other reasons.
In "must be true" questions, reject any option that needs outside knowledge or opinion.
Strong vs weak argument

items: Strong: directly about the question, gives a real reason or fact, and matters.
Weak: uses "always / never / only / all" without proof, attacks a person, quotes popularity, or is off the point.

blocks.text: Finding the assumption

items: An assumption is what the speaker takes for granted without saying it.
Test: deny the option. If the statement then makes no sense, it is the assumption.

blocks.text: Example: "Bring your admit card to the exam hall." Assumed: admit cards will be checked at the hall. Deny it ("no one checks") and the notice is pointless.
An option can be true and still not be assumed. Pick only what the statement needs.

items: 1. Write the differences between terms. Constant → arithmetic.
2. Not constant? Take differences of the differences.
3. Growing fast? Try ratios (×2, ×3) or ×n then ± a number.
4. Near squares or cubes? Test n² ± 1, n³ ± 1.
5. Still stuck? Split odd and even places into two series.

blocks.text: Example: 5, 7, 11, 17, 25, ? → differences 2, 4, 6, 8 → next +10 → 35.
Check your rule on every term, not just the first three; "which number is wrong" questions hide one bad term.
EJOTY
Opposite letter = 27 − position (pairs add to 27: A–Z, B–Y, C–X…).
Past Z, wrap round to A: Y + 3 = B (25 + 3 = 28 → 28 − 26 = 2).

items: "Some P are Q" ↔ "Some Q are P" (both ways).
"No P is Q" ↔ "No Q is P" (both ways).
"All P are Q" turns round only as "Some Q are P" (exam convention), never "All Q are P".

blocks.text: "All P are Q" never gives "All Q are P". And "Some P are not Q" cannot be turned round.

items: Rank from bottom = total − rank from top + 1.
Total in a row = left rank + right rank − 1.
Turn right = 90° clockwise (N → E → S → W).
Straight-line distance: Pythagoras; watch for 3-4-5 and 6-8-10.
Blood relations: draw the family tree; mark male and female.

blocks.text: Example: In a class of 35, Sara is 10th from the top → 35 − 10 + 1 = 26th from the bottom.
Example: Ali walks 6 km north, turns right, walks 8 km → 10 km north-east of the start.
Facing south, your right hand points west. Always turn from the way the person is facing, not from north.

items: 1. Draw the slots (seats, floors, days) and list the people.
2. Place fixed clues first ("Ali is in seat 2").
3. Then linked clues ("immediately right of", "opposite").
4. Then negatives ("not in seat 4") to cut the choices.
5. Re-read every clue against the finished grid.

blocks.text: Example: Seats 1–4 in a row, numbered left to right, all facing north. Ali is in seat 2. Sara is immediately right of Ali. Bilal is not in seat 4. Where is Hamza? → Sara 3; Bilal must take 1; Hamza is in seat 4.
"Immediately right" means the very next seat; "to the right" means anywhere on that side.
Round table, all facing the centre: a person's right is the anticlockwise direction.

head: Code type
Example
rows: "ka lo" = red pen, "lo mi" = pen box → lo = pen

blocks.text: For word codes, find the word the two sentences share; the code they share stands for it.
Test the rule on every letter. Wrong options often get the first two letters right and the rest wrong.
Decoding (code → word)? Run the rule backwards: if the code adds 1, subtract 1.

title: Does a course of action follow?

blocks.text: An action follows only if it passes all three tests:

items: 1. Relevant: it tackles the problem in the statement.
2. Practical: it can really be done by the people named.
3. Proportionate: not extreme, and does not punish innocent people.

blocks.text: Example: Patients wait hours at a hospital because only one registration counter is open. I. Open more counters at busy hours. II. Close the outpatient department. → Only I follows.
An immediate fix and a step to stop it happening again can both follow → "Both I and II follow".
Judge only from the statement. Do not reject a sensible action just because it costs money.

title: Flag words in courses of action

blocks.text: Example: A few students used phones in a test. "Ban phones in the whole city" fails; "check bags before future tests" follows.
Flag words are a first filter, not proof. Always re-check the action against the exact problem.

title: Cause and effect: the four verdicts

blocks.text: Ask: Which came first? Can one directly produce the other? Could one third event explain both?

head: Verdict
Example pair
rows: I is the cause, II its effect
I. Snow blocked the mountain pass. II. Fruit trucks could not reach the town.
II is the cause, I its effect
I. The shop's fridge stopped working. II. The shop's power was cut.
I. Schools in the city closed. II. Offices in the city closed. (e.g. a storm warning)
Both are effects of independent causes
I. A Karachi team won a match. II. A bridge opened in Swat.

blocks.text: Two events on the same day are not cause and effect unless one can really bring about the other.
Superstitions and weak cause claims usually rest on one of these:

items: Coincidence: two things happened together once or twice.
Selective memory: only the matching cases are remembered.
Hidden third factor: hot weather raises both ice-cream sales and fan sales.
No mechanism: nothing links the "cause" to the result.

blocks.text: Example: Umar thinks his green cap makes his cricket team win. Best answer: a cap worn by a spectator has no way to change how the players play.
An answer that mocks the believer ("only foolish people think so") is weak: it attacks the person, not the claim.
For positive thinking, pick the option showing effort changes the result.
